title: blackboard-interview-ramsey-alvarez-reflection
content:
Quick after-interview blackboard for Ramsey Alvarez (applied: runtime capacity engineer)

Context and setup:
- 60m loop: 20m system design, 20m take-home problem walkthrough, 20m culture/operations.
- Role focus: predictable throughput, KV cache strategies, and rollout safety for Dedicated offering.
- Interviewers: Jonas Keller (me), Aisha Rahman (SRE), Diego Ramos (serving runtime).

First impressions / signal map:
- Communicated at a calm pace, uses whiteboard to anchor ideas rather than rambling.
- Strong mental models about trade-offs: availability vs. predictability, batching vs. latency.
- Good appreciation for operational constraints (SLOs, cost), kept returning to SLO-first reasoning — high signal.

System design notes (20m):
- Proposed split-queues per tenant with dynamic sharding keyed by request-rate percentiles. Reasoning: isolates noisy-tenants and simplifies burst isolation.
- Suggested an admission controller that applies backpressure when queue depth + tail latency > threshold (nice concrete trigger).
- KV cache: advocated for prefix-aware caching + per-model LRU with adaptive TTLs based on observed token reuse. Mentioned tradeoff: cache coherence on model rollouts (didn’t fully flesh out invalidation).
- Observability: recommended per-request trace ids, sampling heuristics tied to SLA breaches, and lightweight token-counting metrics.

Take-home exercise walkthrough (20m):
- Candidate walked through a simplified batching controller they’d prototype: feedback loop uses recent quantiles to expand/contract batch windows. Clear pseudo-code on back-of-envelope, but skipped edge case: tail-quantile under sudden spike.
- Brought up variant: optimistic batching with fallback to synchronous path if latency SLO violated — pragmatic and grounded in real constraints.
- Implementation notes: suggested using a ring buffer + worker pool; mentioned potential lock contention and suggested lock-free queues in hot paths.

Culture / ops fit (20m):
- Emphasized building within product constraints and asking for shipping minimal viable safety features first (e.g., global kill switch, per-tenant rate caps).
- Good collaborator anecdotes: description of working across infra and product to sunset a legacy batching daemon — concrete and believable.
- Risk: tends to default to engineering-simplicity over long-tail correctness; asked clarifying Qs but didn't volunteer extensive testing strategies (gap).

Risks & unknowns:
- Rollout invalidation: didn’t outline a robust strategy for cache invalidation when models change versions; this is important for our rollouts.
- Spike behavior: controller sketch is solid for steady-state, weaker on burst handling and safety under cascading failures.
- Scale experience: unclear number of GPUs / single-tenant scale they’ve operated at — asked but answer vague.

Signal summary (quick):
- Technical problem solving: 7/10 (practical, some missing edge cases)
- System design/architecture: 7/10 (good trade-offs, missing rollout coherency)
- Coding/implementation intuition: 6/10 (clear pseudo-code, less on testing harnesses)
- Ownership & communication: 8/10 (good cross-team stories, product-first thinking)

Suggested next steps / interview cadence:
- Engineering follow-up: a short pairing session to push on cache invalidation + burst scenarios (45m pairing). Purpose: see their debugging/testing approach and how they iterate on controller heuristics.
- If pairing looks good: pass to hiring manager loop with a focus on past scale metrics (what throughput and p99s they managed).

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Ping Diego for kernel-level concurrency nuance (did candidate's lock-free suggestions map to our runtime constraints?).
- Drop a small homework prompt if we want more concrete evidence: give a trace with bursts and ask for parameter tuning for the batching controller (evaluate before pairing).
- Capture a one-paragraph summary for hiring committee: short, neutral, include signals + risks.

One-paragraph blurb (for panel):
Ramsey Alvarez showed solid practical instincts for runtime engineering — good trade-off framing and concrete proposals for batching and caching. Strong communicator and product-aware. Key concerns are rollout cache coherence and burst/safety handling; recommend a technical pairing to validate edge-case thinking before advancing.

Random jots & micro-quotables:
- "I'd rather have a simple global kill switch than a fragile hundred-flag rollout" — pragmatic ops mindset.
- Asked about telemetry cost: "we should sample aggressively but stratify by tenant signal" — shows awareness of cost/observability trade-offs.

End.
